1:
Bildad's demand whether God could pervert judgment draws from Job not a rebuttal but an unexpected assent, and the witnesses gather around the strange courtesy with which the sufferer opens his reply. The reformed John Gill marks the graciousness of it: without so much as noticing Bildad's harsh expressions and severe censures, or his unfriendliness, Job enters directly into the argument, granting some things, confuting others, and defending himself and his conduct. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same generosity in the concession. Bildad had begun with a rebuke for talking so much, which Job might easily have retorted; but on the principle Bildad had laid down, that God never perverts judgment, Job frankly agrees — "I know it is so of a truth." We should be ready, Henry urges, to own how far we agree with those we dispute with, and not slight, much less resist, a truth though produced by an adversary and urged against us, but receive it in the light and love of it, however it may have been misapplied.

The latin-fathers Gregory the Great turns this very forbearance into a portrait of the good hearer. The hearts of the good, whose dislike rises not at the speaker but at the offence, sit as "the most even umpires" in deciding an opponent's words: they so reject what is put forth amiss that they still set the seal upon whatever they recognise to be delivered in truth, for among a wilderness of thorns the ear of corn is generally found growing from good seed, and must be cherished by the tiller's hand even while the thorn is plucked up. So Job, hearing Bildad's true and forcible sentiments against the wicked in general, treads under foot the prosecution of his own defence and sanctions the truth he had heard: for "man put with God is not justified" — man being put under God receives righteousness, but being put with God, comparing himself with the Author of all good, he loses it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the movement the whole chapter will follow: Job acknowledges God's justice and man's sinfulness, celebrates the almighty power manifested in earth and heaven, maintains that God afflicts the innocent as well as the wicked without respect to their works, and at last complains of his own lot while still holding fast his integrity. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the frame for all that follows, in which a man who has just lost everything begins his reply not by accusing God of injustice but by confessing that no flesh can be just before him.
2:
Job's opening words own the very maxim Bildad had pressed, yet the witnesses watch that confession of God's justice turn at once into the deeper question that will drive the chapter — "how should man be just with God?" The reformed John Gill fixes the certainty of the assent: Job knew this "of a truth," most certainly, that God is just and holy in all his ways and works, whether of providence or grace; a man enlightened by the spirit of wisdom and revelation, he needed no instruction in this article, and kept it in sight amidst all his afflictions, ready to acknowledge it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear a touch of irony in the confirmation: "yea, indeed, I know it is thus." Job does not refer to the like saying of Eliphaz at Job 4:17 but assents to Bildad's chief thought, that God does not pervert what is right; what God does is always right because God does it, and how then could man maintain himself just in opposition to God? Should God enter into controversy with him, he could not give information on one of a thousand subjects, but would be so confounded, so disarmed by reason, that he could not answer.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the confession against man's littleness. Adam Clarke acknowledges the general truth of the friends' maxims — God will not ultimately punish the righteous nor let the wicked finally triumph — yet adds that, righteous before men and truly sincere in his piety as he was, "when compared with the immaculate holiness of God, all my righteousness is nothing." John Wesley reads the same double note: Job knew that God is just in all his ways, ordinarily blessing the righteous and punishing the wicked, and knew too that no man is absolutely just if God be severe to mark what is amiss in him.

Here a real difference of temper divides the readers. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry grants that some understand the words as a passionate complaint of God's strictness and severity, a God there is no dealing with — and he owns that peevish expressions do escape Job in this chapter. But Henry takes it rather as a pious confession of man's sinfulness, and Job's own in particular: that if God should deal with any of us according to the desert of our iniquities we should certainly be undone, for "in his sight shall no flesh living be justified." The witnesses thus circle a genuine ambiguity — whether the cry "how should man be just with God?" is Job's murmur against an overwhelming judge, or his humble owning that the creature has no plea — even as they agree that the confession of God's justice is sincere and settled.
3:
The impossibility of arguing a case with God takes shape in the image of a thousand questions to which man has not one answer, and the witnesses press both the law-court metaphor and the sting hidden in the number. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the dispute at length: God can ask a thousand puzzling questions which those who quarrel with him cannot answer — as when he spoke out of the whirlwind at Job 38 and asked, "Dost thou know this? Canst thou do that?" to none of which Job could reply; and God can lay to our charge a thousand offences, draw up a thousand articles of impeachment, and we cannot set one aside as foreign, another as frivolous, another as false, but must by silence give consent that they are all true, laying our hand upon our mouth as Job would at Job 40:4 and cry, Guilty.

The reformed John Gill takes the contention either way and finds it hopeless: whether God contend with man, entering a controversy in law to dispute whether he is just, or man contend with God — a potsherd striving with its maker — the match is unequal, and there is no striving with God in a judicial way. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke drives it to the conscience: God is so holy and his law so strict that of a thousand offences of which a man may be accused he cannot vindicate himself even in one; how little that any man does, even in righteousness, truth, and mercy, can stand the penetrating eye of a just and holy God when all motives and objects come to be scrutinised — and so, he cries, how necessary to fallen man is the doctrine of justification by faith. John Wesley reads it simply as "one accusation among a thousand which God shall produce against him."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lets the phrase carry two senses at once: if man choose to contend with God, he cannot answer him "one question of a thousand, once in a thousand times" — whether one demand out of the multitude God might put, or one instance out of a thousand encounters. The witnesses converge on the futility of the suit and differ only in accent: to Henry it is the thousand unanswerable questions of an omniscient judge, to Gill the vanity of the potsherd's plea, to Clarke the thousand offences no man can clear, to Ellicott the numberless times the creature must fall silent — but all read a court in which man, summoned, has nothing to say.
4:
Two attributes — wisdom of heart and might of strength — become for the witnesses the double reason no creature can win either the argument or the war with God. The reformed John Gill dwells on the wisdom: God is originally, essentially, and perfectly wise, the only all-wise God whose understanding is infinite, able to traverse all the schemes of men and disappoint all their devices, so that against his counsel no wisdom or understanding avails; he is so knowing that he sees all that is in man, every thought of the heart, every word of the tongue, every action of the life, and will bring each into judgment — how then can sinful men be just in the sight of so wise and holy a Being upon the score of a righteousness of their own?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the challenge of the second clause: "who hath hardened himself against him and hath prospered?" The answer is very easy, for no instance can be produced from the beginning of the world of any daring sinner who hardened himself against God and did not find him too hard for him, and pay dearly for his folly. Apostate angels hardened themselves and did not prosper, as 2 Peter 2:4 records; the dragon fights, but is cast out at Revelation 12:9; and all the opposition men give to God is but setting briers and thorns before a consuming fire, so foolish, so fruitless, so destructive is the attempt, as in Isaiah 27:4. Wicked men dispute his wisdom and resist the strivings of his Spirit, but they do not prosper; they are only treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke joins the two attributes into a single sentence of judgment: by his infinite knowledge God searches out and sees all things, and by his almighty power he can punish all delinquencies, so that "he that rebels against him must be destroyed." The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as Job's own confession, wrung from a man in torment who might have been expected to curse God and instead sets himself to honour him: that the God with whom we have to do can neither be outwitted, being wise in heart, nor overpowered, being mighty in strength, and that to think of contending with such a One at law or in combat is the greatest madness a creature can attempt.
5:
The first instance of that might is drawn from the mountains, the very emblem of permanence, and the witnesses divide over whether Job describes literal upheavals or the sheer reach of divine power. The reformed John Gill weighs both. Taken literally, history furnishes instances — a village in Helvetia, he reports from Scheuchzer, swallowed up in 1618 with eighteen hundred souls under a mountain's sudden fall, no trace of it left; and Scripture itself foretells the removal of the Mount of Olives, half to the north and half to the south, at Zechariah 14:4; and at the universal deluge, which covered the tops of the highest hills, some mountains may well have been washed from their places. Or the words may be understood proverbially, of the Lord's mighty power that could remove them if he would.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the wonder against the mountains' proverbial fixedness: nothing is more firm than the mountains, called therefore everlasting; when we speak of removing them we mean the impossible, yet the divine power can make them change their seat — "he removes them, and they know not," whether they will or no. He made Sinai shake in Psalm 68:8, the hills skipped in Psalm 114:4, the everlasting mountains were scattered at Habakkuk 3:6; he can spread the mountains as easily as the husbandman spreads the molehills, be they ever so high and rocky.

The wesleyan-arminian voices lean toward the earthquake. Adam Clarke refers the verse to those strong convulsions in which mountains, valleys, and whole islands are removed in an instant, and reads "they know not" of the suddenness — the work done in the twinkling of an eye, no warning given, the mountain visible and invisible in the same moment. John Wesley takes it the same way, that God removes them "suddenly and unexpectedly," ascribing sense to them by a figure, and reads "in his anger" as the token of his displeasure with the men who live upon them. So the debate stands: whether Job points to actual convulsions — the Flood, the earthquake, the coming rending of Olivet — or paints, in the removal of what cannot be moved, a picture of the power against which it is madness to contend. Henry lets both stand: it is enough to say Job speaks of what God can do, though if we must read it of fact, the flood best answers the description.
6:
From the mountains Job passes to the earth itself and its unseen supports, and the witnesses read the trembling pillars as both the terror of earthquake and a sign of the last dissolution. The reformed John Gill lifts the eye to the end of all things: God can shake the earth out of her place, and will at the last day, when it shall be utterly dissolved, reel to and fro like a drunkard, be removed as a cottage, and flee away from the face of him that sits upon the throne, as John saw in Revelation 20:11. This cannot mean ordinary earthquakes, which are only partial and shake but some parts; it may glance too at the Flood, when the earth, as Burnet's Theory supposes, received some change in its situation, a thing the apostle hints when he distinguishes the present earth, reserved unto fire, from the former, at 2 Peter 3:7.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole strophe into one sweep of solitary omnipotence — he shakes the earth from her place and the pillars tremble, commands the sun and it rises not, seals up the stars, alone spreads out the heavens and treads upon the heights of the sea — reading it all as the field of a divine action that upholds and overturns the frame of the world at will. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps closer to the ground: "the pillars thereof tremble" refers to an earthquake and to that tremulous motion which sometimes gives warning of the coming catastrophe, from which the convulsion takes its very name. He notes that in Scripture-language earthquakes may signify violent commotions in states, mountains stand for rulers, the sun for empires, the stars for petty states — but he judges the expressions here most likely literal.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the two lines plainly: "the earth" means great portions of it, shaken by earthquakes or by the removing of islands; and "the pillars thereof" are the deep and inward parts which, like pillars, support the visible surface we tread. The witnesses do not sharply divide; they hold together the near and the far — the ground that quakes under a man's feet in his own day, and the whole creation that will one day be shaken out of its place — and let both proclaim the same power, that what seems most immovably to support the world will itself need support when God gives it a shock.
7:
The sun's unfailing rising and the fixed shining of the stars, the surest of nature's constants, are named next as things God can suspend at a word, and the witnesses gather instances of the constant made to fail. The reformed John Gill runs through them. God could do it if he would, as he made the sun stand still in the days of Joshua at Joshua 10, and brought the shadow back ten degrees for Hezekiah in Isaiah 38:8; or the sense is that the sun rises only when and where God commands, and never else; or it looks to eclipses, or to the sun's being covered with clouds in tempestuous weather so that it seems not risen; or to the three days' darkness in Egypt, which fell about Job's time, at Exodus 10:22; or rather to the general flood, when it rained forty days and forty nights, during all which the sun appeared not, as if it were not risen.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads both clauses of a heaven blotted out: God "commandeth the sun" — obscures it with clouds, with thick darkness, or with an eclipse — and "sealeth up the stars," as the contents of a letter are wrapped and sealed so that they cannot be read; sometimes the heavens become black as ebony, and no star, figure, or character in this great book of God can be made out. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on that last verb: comparing the scales sealed shut at Job 41:15, he finds in "sealing" the idea of shutting up, of taking away the power of a thing, so that the stars are not merely hidden but stopped, their light and influence withdrawn.

The witnesses do not divide over the sense, only over how far to press the fact. Whether Job recalls actual darkenings — the long day at Gibeon, the plague over Egypt, the drowned world of Noah — or speaks in the language of what God can do at any hour, they agree the verse strips heaven of its two great certainties. The sun that never yet missed its appointed rising, and the stars that never yet failed to shed their light, are held in a hand that can command the one to stay below the horizon and seal the others in the dark; and if the most regular works of nature hang thus on the divine word, how much more do the hidden ways of providence, over which Job is contending, lie wholly at God's disposal.
8:
Two acts of solitary omnipotence — the stretching out of the heavens and the treading of the sea — draw the witnesses into the imagery and a quiet dispute over the Hebrew. The reformed John Gill takes the first of continuance rather than first creation: the word rendered "spreadeth out" is named from being expanded, and points to the ether or atmosphere spread around us like a curtain and a tent to dwell in, as in Psalm 104:2; God not only spread the heavens once but keeps them spread, that they be not rolled up as a scroll, and this he does "alone," without the help of any creature. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh a rival reading here. Ewald and Hirzel, following Psalm 18, would render the line of God letting down the clouds of heaven and walking high above the towering thunder-clouds, on the heights of the cloud-sea; but the parallel passages — Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 104:2, and above all Isaiah 44:24 — show that the first clause speaks of the creation of the firmament, so that the verb must mean to expand, and the waters in view are those divided by the expanse.

On the treading of the sea the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds a very majestic image: God not only walks upon the waters, but when the sea runs mountains high he steps from billow to billow in his almighty and essential majesty. He sets beside it David's word that the Lord sitteth upon the flood at Psalm 29:10, and judges the psalmist to outdo Job when he sings that God "did fly upon the wings of the wind" — "Job is great, but in every respect David is greater." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase literally "high place of the sea," the sea when and where it runs mountains high, and reads earthquake, eclipse, and hurricane together as the field of divine action.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley hears in the whole a description of a black and tempestuous season, when the heavens seem brought down nearer the earth, and takes "treadeth" to mean that God represses and rules the waters when they rage, for treading upon a thing signifies in Scripture the using of power and dominion over it. So the witnesses land on a real difference — whether God is pictured walking the storm-tossed sea underfoot, as Clarke, Ellicott, and Wesley read it, or striding the cloud-heights above the thunder, as Ewald and Hirzel would have it — while agreeing that the same hand which stretched and holds the heavens holds the raging sea in subjection.
9:
The constellations named here — the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, with the chambers of the south — open the widest philological debate of the chapter, and the witnesses crowd around the identity of the stars and what the old Hebrew names really mean. The reformed John Gill takes "Arcturus" not for a single star but for a collection, a constellation, citing Bar Tzemach and Ben Melech and the "Arcturus and his sons" of Job 38:32; it lies about the northern pole, in the tail of the Bear, appears in September, and brings stormy weather, though he notes that Aben Ezra took the word rather for the seven stars usually reckoned the Pleiades.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke spreads out the whole history of the rendering: the Septuagint gives Pleiades, Hesperus, Arcturus, and Orion; the Vulgate Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades; the Targum, Syriac, and Arabic differ again; Coverdale has "the waynes of heaven, the Orions, the vii starres," the German "the wagon of heaven, Orion, and the clucking hen." But Clarke inclines to Parkhurst and Bate, who deny that constellations are meant at all: kimah, from a root to be warm, denotes genial heat; ash, a parching, biting air; kesil, the rigid, contracting cold; and the "chambers of the south" the thick clouds — so that the verse names the weathers, not the stars. He reports too that Dr. Hales, taking kimah and kesil for Taurus and Scorpio, would fix Job's very date at 2337 years before Christ; but such a system, Clarke warns, is built on the unproved assumption that these words are constellations at all.

The grammatical-historical voices keep to the stars. Charles Ellicott finds in the specific names a proof that the writer's countrymen had attained real knowledge of astronomy — the Great Bear the glory of the northern hemisphere, Orion of the southern sky, the Pleiades of the east, and the "chambers" the unknown, unexplored regions of which the speaker has no experience. Keil and Delitzsch render simply "the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, and the chambers of the south." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley names these as constellations of greatest eminency, under which he comprehends all the stars: Arcturus a northern constellation near the Bear, Orion more southerly and rising in December, the Pleiades the seven stars, and the inmost "chambers of the south" those stars toward the southern pole that are for the most part hidden from these parts of the world. So the debate is genuinely three-cornered — whether Ash, Kesil, and Kimah name the great constellations, or, with Parkhurst and Bate, the qualities of heat and cold and cloud, or, with Hales, Taurus and Scorpio precisely enough to date the book — and the witnesses agree only that the God who made them, by whatever names, holds all the host of heaven at his appointment.
10:
Having surveyed the heavens Job turns to providence, borrowing — as the witnesses are quick to notice — the very words his opponent Eliphaz had used. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott points to the echo without comment beyond the fact: in saying that God "doeth great things," Job adopts the exact language his former antagonist Eliphaz had spoken at Job 5:9. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the significance of the borrowing: Job says the same as Eliphaz, and in the original in the very same words, on purpose to show his full agreement with him touching the divine perfections, so that their quarrel is not over the greatness of God but over the meaning of Job's affliction.

The reformed John Gill opens out the sweep of the phrase. God does "great things past finding out" in heaven and in earth, great as to quantity and quality, works that cannot be thoroughly searched out so as to tell their number or express their nature to the full — what he has done and does in creation, in providence, and in grace, each a field of wonders past reckoning. The unsearchableness is not a defect in the works but the mark of their Author, whose doings overflow every measure the creature can bring.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weaves the two threads together — the greatness of the works and the grace of the concession. When Job comes to speak of God's providence he says that he does many things and great, many and great to admiration, and he says it in words he does not decline to take up after his adversary, though Eliphaz is now his opponent; for a truth is not the less true for coming from one who has misapplied it. Henry marvels at the depth the phrase opens: God's works of wonder are so many that we cannot number them and so mysterious that we cannot find them out — "O the depth of his counsels!" The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as a hinge between the two kingdoms Job has been surveying, the kingdom of nature just described and the kingdom of providence now to be entered, and they find in Job's willingness to echo Eliphaz a quiet proof that the sufferer, for all his anguish, is contending not against the God whose greatness he confesses but against the friends who have wielded that greatness as a weapon.
11:
"Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not" — from what God does Job turns to how he works, invisibly, passing close yet unperceived, and the witnesses read the verse as the sublime confession of a majesty that can never be brought to trial. The reformed John Gill unfolds the invisibility by degrees: though the angels always behold his face, and men see his eternal power and Godhead in the works of creation, and saints by faith have a comfortable view of his countenance in the person of Christ, the image of the invisible God, and shall in heaven see him as he is — yet his essence remains invisible, not only unseen by bodily eyes but incomprehensible to the mind, so that he passes and Job cannot trace him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the confession on the ground of God's very nature: "he is incomprehensible in all his ways and in all his works; and he must be so if he be God, and work as God, for his own nature and his operations are past finding out." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott again catches Job echoing his opponents, for "he passeth on also" is an expression Eliphaz had used at Job 4:15; and he hears in the words of great sublimity here the depicting of a God omnipotent yet invisible, and the utter hopelessness of entering into judgment with him. Yet this, Ellicott observes, though a proposition to which all must assent, is virtually the one most often contravened, for men still cast about to justify themselves before God and will do so till the end of time; and it is in teaching such as this that the Book of Job has laid the foundation of the Gospel, preparing for its acceptance by overthrowing man's natural and habitual standing-ground in himself.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the two verbs of God's dealings with men: "he goeth" — he works by his providence in ways of mercy or of judgment; "he passeth" — he goes from place to place, from one action to another, spoken after the manner of men. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse marks the exact reason Job cannot make his part good at law: not that God is unjust, but that he is invisible and incomprehensible, moving past the sufferer unseen and unperceived, so that a man can neither summon such a One to a hearing nor follow the paths of a providence whose way is in the sea and whose footsteps are not known.
12:
"Behold, he taketh away, who can hinder him?" — the sovereignty that no creature can arraign is put in a double question, who can stay God's hand, and who dare call him to account. The reformed John Gill first marks what God never takes from his people — his love, in which he always rests; his grace, once wrought; the unspeakable gift of his Son and every spiritual blessing in Christ, all irreversible and irrevocable — and then what he takes at pleasure, the temporal blessings: so he had taken away Job's children and servants, his substance and wealth, and his bodily health, and, when it pleases him, takes a man himself out of the world, as the Targum and Gersom read the last clause. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the words an incontestable sovereignty: whatever goes, it is God who takes it, and by whatever hand it is removed, his hand must be owned in the removing — "the Lord takes away, and who can hinder him?" or, as the margin has it, who shall make him restore? God is not obliged to give us a reason of what he does; the meanings of his proceedings we know not now, but it will be time enough to know hereafter, when it will appear that what seemed done by prerogative was done in infinite wisdom, as at Daniel 4:35, where none may say unto him, What doest thou?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke softens the taking into a lending: God "never gives, but he is ever lending"; while the gift is useful or improved he lets it remain, but when it becomes useless or is misused he recalls it — and "who can cause him to restore it?" He is supreme, and will give account of none of his matters; infinitely wise, and cannot mistake; infinitely kind, and can do nothing cruel; infinitely good, and can do nothing wrong, so that none should question either his motives or his operations. The grammatical-historical voices set the sovereignty in its widest frame. Keil and Delitzsch say God works among men as he works in nature, with a supreme control over all, invisibly and irresistibly, not responsible to any being, as at Isaiah 45:9. Charles Ellicott presses the harder edge: even putting the case that God were, so to say, in the wrong and the assailant, yet even then he would maintain his cause from sheer might and crush his adversary. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws Job's own inference: if God determines to take away a man's children, servants, or estate, who can restrain him or dare reprove him? — "far be it from me to quarrel with God, whereof you untruly accuse me."
13:
The last note of the nature-and-providence hymn is God's irresistible anger, before which even the mightiest confederates collapse, and the witnesses puzzle over the shadowy "helpers of Rahab" that stoop beneath it. The reformed John Gill reads the anger two ways according to its objects: God seems angry with his own people when he afflicts them and hides his face, yet this does not always last, for he does not retain anger for ever but with everlasting kindness has mercy; but with the wicked he is angry every day, and from them he never withdraws his anger, punishing them with everlasting destruction, to which fire his wrath is compared. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes God the Lord of his own anger, who lets it out or calls it in according to his will; and if he will not withdraw it, "the proud helpers do stoop under him" — he certainly breaks and crushes those who proudly help one another against him. Proud men set themselves against God and join hand in hand, the kings of the earth and the rulers taking counsel together as in Psalm 2; but unless he please to withdraw his anger, in the day of his patience, the proud helpers stoop and fall with those they designed to help. "Who knows the power of God's anger?"

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lifts the veil on the phrase itself: "proud helpers" is literally "helpers of Rahab," a name found at Isaiah 30:7 and Psalm 87:4 — but whether Rahab here is Egypt, so that a probable allusion lies to the overthrow of Pharaoh and his hosts, or a poetical name for the lost archangel, it is impossible to say; the expression is used to express the very ideal of strength, the race of the giants. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep to the plain sense of the crushing. Adam Clarke: "it is of no use to contend with God; he cannot be successfully resisted; all his opposers must perish." John Wesley glosses the "helpers" as those who undertake to uphold and defend one another against him, and "stoop" as to fall and be crushed by him. So the witnesses agree that the mightiest confederacy of strength is nothing before the divine anger, and divide only over the identity of Rahab's helpers — whether the drowned power of Egypt, the fallen angelic host, or simply the proud giant-strength of any who league themselves against God — the very consideration that presses Job to his despairing inference in the verse that follows.
14:
Having magnified a God who crushes the proud helpers, Job draws the crushing inference for himself — if such confederates stoop, how shall one feeble man frame an answer? The reformed John Gill gathers up all that has gone before: God is wise in heart and mighty in strength, invisible, passing by unseen so that there is no knowing where to speak to him, and sovereign to do whatever he pleases; and if the great men of the earth, proud tyrants, and even the infernal principalities and powers are made to stoop to him, how should so poor, weak, and feeble a creature as Job enter the lists, contend with God, and answer to any charge or article exhibited against him? Here Job speaks as meanly of himself as he had spoken highly of God, between whom there is no comparison at all.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry applies to Job what he had said of man in general: he durst not dispute with God. "If the proud helpers stoop under him, how much less shall I — a poor weak creature, so far from being a helper that I am very helpless — answer him? What can I say against what God does?" If the potter make the clay into a vessel of dishonour, or break in pieces the vessel he has made, shall the clay or the broken vessel reason with him? So absurd is the man who replies against God, or thinks to talk the matter out with him; rather let all flesh be silent before him.

The wesleyan-arminian voices strike the same note of unequal terms. Adam Clarke reads it as the confession, "I cannot contend with my Maker; he is the Lawgiver and the Judge; how shall I stand in judgment before him?" John Wesley presses it home: since no creature can resist his power and no man can comprehend his counsels and ways, how can Job contend with him, or answer the allegations and arguments produced against him? The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the pivot at which Job turns the great confession of God's wisdom and might inward upon himself, so that the very attributes he has celebrated become the reasons he dare not so much as choose out his words to reason with such a One — a humility real and deep, even as the darker note of the following verses shows how near it lies, in his present anguish, to despair of a fair hearing.
15:
Even on the supposition of his own innocence Job renounces all thought of answering, and turns from assertion to entreaty — "whom, though I were righteous, yet would I not answer, but I would make supplication to my judge." The reformed John Gill is careful which righteousness Job here disclaims: not the righteousness of his cause, which he strongly held, nor the evangelic righteousness of his living Redeemer, by which he knew he should be justified and by which a believer may indeed answer God, pleading Christ's righteousness against every charge; but his own legal and civil righteousness, which he will not urge before God, since on that ground no man living can be justified. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the very soul of humility: "though clear of all the crimes of which you accuse me, yet I would not dare to stand before his immaculate holiness"; man's holiness may profit man, but in the sight of the infinite purity of God it is nothing, and, not conscious of any sin, Job would still not think himself thereby justified, but would cry, from a sense of the exceeding breadth of the commandment, "Cleanse thou me from secret faults."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the alternative sharply: Job now puts the case that he were actually righteous, and yet even then supplication, and not assertion, would best become him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the ground of that choice: though not conscious to himself of any sin, Job durst not undertake to plead his cause against God or maintain his integrity before him, because God knows him better than he knows himself; and so he would only make supplication, that God would judge favourably of him and his cause, and not deal with him according to the rigour of his justice.

The witnesses do not divide, and the theology they gather is exact. A man may be righteous before his fellows and yet have nothing to say before God, not because God is unjust but because his holiness is a light that discovers faults the conscience never marked. The puritan-evangelical reading of the same movement, that Job knew too much of God to stand a trial with him and too much of himself to insist on his own justification, runs beneath all the rest: the innocent man's wisest posture is not to answer his Judge but to beseech him, casting himself on mercy rather than merit, and waiving the plea of a righteousness that could not survive the scrutiny of the all-seeing eye.
16:
Job carries the thought further into a strange distrust — that even if he called and were answered, he could not believe the answer was for his own sake. The reformed John Gill hears in the words both a present doubt and a past experience. Broughton would read them as a question, "if I cry, will he answer me?" — as though Job, still under the heavy hand of God, doubted whether he would be heard; yet Job was a praying man who had often found God a God hearing and answering prayer, for himself and his children and his friends, and now only questions whether he would be answered in this extremity. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it of the sheer disproportion between the suppliant and the sought: "I could scarcely suppose, such is his majesty and such his holiness, that he could condescend to notice a being so mean, and in every respect so infinitely beneath his notice" — a sentiment which, Clarke adds, sufficiently confutes the friends' slander that Job was presumptuous and had no becoming notion of the majesty of God.

The puritan-evangelical reading, drawn from Job's own words, turns the verse into a lesson on the grounds of accepted prayer. Job had no reason to think there was anything in his prayers to recommend them to the divine acceptance, or to fetch in an answer of peace — no worth or worthiness to which to ascribe their success, which must be attributed purely to the grace and compassion of God, who answers before we call and not because we call, and gives gracious answers to our prayers, but not for our prayers. So even if God had granted the thing asked, Job would not believe that his own voice had been hearkened to, but would own that it was done purely for God's own name's sake. Bishop Patrick reads it to the same effect: had Job made supplication and had his desire granted, he would not think his prayer had done the business.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the disbelief of a man still under the tokens of displeasure: Job could not believe that God had indeed granted his desire, because he was still full of the marks of God's anger, and would therefore conclude it was but a pleasant dream and not a real thing. The witnesses do not divide; they read a verse in which the sense of God's majesty and of his own unworthiness has grown so heavy that Job can scarce credit even the mercy of being heard — a distrust that, whatever of unbelief clings to it, springs from no low thought of God but from too overwhelming a sense of the distance between the holy Judge and the suppliant at his feet.
17:
The distrust deepens into a bitter picture of God as an adversary who wounds without ceasing — "he breaketh me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause." The reformed John Gill hears in the storm an image drawn from Job's own calamity: a tempest that rises suddenly, comes powerfully, and carries all before it irresistibly, perhaps with reference to the very wind that blew down the house upon his children; and he notes Schultens's rendering of a "burning tempest," such as the eastern travellers describe, which kills a man at once and blackens his flesh like a coal, so that it comes off the bones at a touch — a man broken to pieces indeed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the rare verb "breaketh," found, he observes, in only three passages of Scripture — here, in the bruising of the serpent's head at Genesis 3:15, and in the covering darkness of Psalm 139:11 — so that the word itself carries a weight of violence.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays the stress on the closing "without cause": the Targum, Syriac, and Arabic have God smiting even every hair of Job's head and multiplying his wounds for no reason known to himself or any man; and it is therefore cruel and illogical, Clarke insists, to assert that Job suffers for his crimes, when the very text he speaks denies any adequate cause. John Wesley reads the same phrase with a needed distinction: not that the affliction was without any desert of Job's at all, but without any special cause of such singular sufferings, without the peculiar and extraordinary guilt his friends charged him with; and the "breaking" he takes as unexpected, violent, and, to Job's own apprehension, irrecoverable.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the strophe that follows into one movement: God would rather crush him in a tempest and multiply his wounds without cause, would not suffer him to take his breath but fill him with bitter things — a description not of what God is, but of how God's dealings appear to a man overwhelmed. The witnesses do not divide over the fact of the suffering, and they agree on the point that matters most against the friends: that the wounds are multiplied "without cause," so that the storm which has broken Job is no proof of the secret wickedness they impute to him. Yet here, the puritan reading elsewhere warns, Job spoke unadvisedly with his lips, reflecting on God's justice in saying that it was all without cause — a passion the following verses will only heighten.
18:
The catalogue of the tempest continues with a complaint that God allows no pause between the blows — "he will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness." The reformed John Gill considers whether the words point to Job's disease, an asthma or quinsy that hindered his breathing, but inclines rather to the hot burning winds of those countries, which sometimes blow so strongly as almost to take a man's breath away, as the traveller reports of the wind between Suez and Cairo, so fierce that men must turn their backs to it to draw breath at all. The design, Gill says, is to show that Job's afflictions were continued and without interval, repeated so fast and coming so thick, one after another, that he had no breathing time.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same relentlessness in body and mind together: "I have no respite in my afflictions; I suffer continually in my body, and my mind is incessantly harassed." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns on the exact action of the phrase — the drawing of breath again after complete exhaustion, the recovering of breath and the power to breathe — and carries the thought forward into the argument it prepares: if Job should say, "I am perfect," the very saying would prove him perverse, because for man to maintain his righteousness before God is at once to proclaim his iniquity, since the finite cannot come into competition with the Infinite nor measure itself therewith. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it simply: "my pains are continual, and I have not so much as a breathing time free from them."

The witnesses do not divide. They read a verse whose grievance is not a single stroke but the unbroken succession of strokes, the denial of that momentary ease in which a sufferer might gather himself; and they agree that the bitterness with which Job says he is filled is the bitterness of a man given no interval to recover. Yet the same reading that hears the truth of the affliction hears also its excess of passion, for Job here, as at his worst, charges God with a cruelty of continuance that the God who does not afflict willingly would not own — the complaint of a good man who at another time would have been far from such hard thoughts, and whom God, considering his frame and the strength of his temptation, will afterward give leave to unsay by repentance.
19:
Job now casts the whole contest in the language of the courts, and finds himself outmatched on both counts, of strength and of right — "if I speak of strength, lo, he is strong; and if of judgment, who shall set me a time to plead?" The reformed John Gill takes the first clause of any appeal to force: were Job to propose carrying his point by might, alas, there is nothing to be done that way, for he is a poor, weak, feeble creature in body, mind, and estate, and there is no disputing with God upon the foot of strength, seeing that even the weakness of God is stronger than men. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes that human wisdom, power, and influence avail nothing before him, and glosses the second clause from the Hebrew — "who would be a witness for me?" or, Who would dare to appear in my behalf? — observing that almost all the terms of this part of the speech are forensic, taken from legal processes and pleadings in the gates or courts of justice.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns the passage so abrupt and enigmatical that its argument is hard to be sure of, though its general drift is plain: "if it were a trial of strength — who is Almighty? and if a matter of judgment, is he not judge and court together? and what authority that he would acknowledge could give me the opportunity of pleading my cause before him?" Were Job righteous, his own mouth would show him wicked; were he perfect, it would prove him perverse. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reduces the two branches to their point: if the cause were to be decided by power, God is stronger than he; if by right, there is no superior judge who can summon them both together and set a time for the pleading.

The witnesses do not divide, and the difficulty they confess is itself instructive. Job is a problem to himself: confident of his innocence, yet confident that his innocence will avail him nothing before God, sure that he must be condemned. It is impossible, Ellicott adds, not to see in this the very attitude the Gospel will afterward vindicate, and impossible fully to enter into Job's position except from the Gospel's standpoint. Here, though, the standpoint is only despair of a hearing: no arbiter can be found to fix an assize between the creature and his Maker, no advocate dare appear, no court is higher than the God who is at once the party, the judge, and the power, so that the suit is lost before it is opened.
20:
"If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me" — the deadlock reaches its sharpest point, where the very attempt to plead innocence becomes the proof of guilt. The reformed John Gill puts the case in its barest form: if Job should seek justification by his own righteousness, trust in himself that he was righteous, and pronounce himself a righteous man, what would it signify? Nothing, for the plea would recoil upon the pleader. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads a deeper submission in it than mere despair: "God must have some reason for his conduct towards me; I therefore do not pretend to justify myself; the attempt would be an insult to his majesty and justice." Though conscious of none of the crimes his friends allege, and knowing no reason why God contends with him, Job grants that God must have some reason, and that reason he does not choose to explain.

The grammatical-historical reading sharpens the paradox to a knife's edge: if Job say, "I am perfect," the word itself shall prove him perverse by the very act of saying so, because for man to maintain his righteousness before God is to proclaim his iniquity, the finite being unable to come into competition with the Infinite. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the plain construction, taking "justify" of Job's pleading against God his own righteousness and innocency, and hearing in the answering clause the certainty that such a plea would be turned back upon him.

The puritan-evangelical reading, drawn from Job's whole posture here, weighs the danger that lies just beneath so humble a confession. A good man, who knows the deceitfulness of his own heart and is jealous over it with a godly jealousy, is suspicious of more evil in himself than he is really conscious of, and therefore will by no means think of justifying himself before God; if we say we have no sin we not only deceive ourselves but affront God, giving the lie to the Scripture which has concluded all under sin. Yet the same reading marks that Job's answer, true as it is to man's inability, begins to imply that the question between the sufferer and the Lord of providence is a question of might and not of right — and there the first evil fruits of a self-righteous spirit appear, which Job will afterwards be reproved for, when he seems ready to condemn God that he may justify himself. The witnesses hold both together: the confession is sound, that no man can plead his own righteousness and stand; but the accent of complaint that creeps into it is the passion Job will have to unsay.
21:
The knot tightens still further in a line the witnesses themselves cannot untie with one hand — "though I were perfect, yet would I not know my soul: I would despise my life." The reformed John Gill takes it as a case merely supposed: though Job were really and truly perfect, conscious of no sin in thought, word, or deed, yet even so he would not stand upon it before God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the genuine division of interpreters. It is usually taken, they report, for an affirmation of innocence made at the peril of Job's own life — "I am innocent, I boldly say it even with scorn of my life," as Schnurrer, Hirzel, Ewald, and Schlottmann read it, taking the clause to mean, I care nothing for my soul. But its first sense, Keil and Delitzsch urge, is rather "I know not my soul, that is, myself"; for the contradiction between his lot and his innocence seems to show that his self-consciousness is deceptive, and makes him a mystery to himself, so that, become a stranger to his own heart, he abhors this life of seeming contradictions and desires nothing less than its long continuance. And the "this is one thing" that follows they do not read as "it is all the same to me whether I live or not," but as "it is all one whether man is innocent or not" — a proposition of which Job takes himself for the proof.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse of a humility that would not trust even its own perfection: had Job the fullest conviction that in every thought, word, and deed he were blameless, yet he would not plead it, nor think it any security for a life of ease, nor any proof that his days should be prolonged. John Wesley draws it the same way: if Job should think himself perfect, yet he would not acknowledge his own soul, nor plead before God the integrity of his soul or life, but would only make supplication to his judge, abhorring or condemning his life rather than trust to any integrity of his own before the pure and piercing eyes of the all-seeing God.

So the witnesses circle a real difficulty in the words themselves — whether Job flings out a bold assertion of innocence in scorn of a life grown hateful to him, as most read it, or, with Keil and Delitzsch, confesses that his very innocence has become a riddle he cannot read, so that he no longer knows his own soul. Both hear beneath it the same weariness of a life that has become offensive to him; and both stop short of the further step, into the charge that God destroys the perfect and the wicked alike, which the next verse will take.
22:
"This is one thing; therefore I said it, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked" — here Job lays down the very thesis that divides him from his friends, and the witnesses weigh both its truth and its heat. The reformed John Gill reads the "one thing" as one event alike to the righteous and the wicked: whether a man be perfect or not, he is equally liable to be afflicted and distressed. On the justice of God, Gill notes, Job agreed with his friends, and believed God righteous even in this; but this one strange and astonishing thing, unaccountable as it was, he could not surrender — that God treats good and bad men alike in the outward dispensations of this life. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry states the dispute exactly: the friends maintained that the righteous always prosper and none but the wicked are in misery; Job asserted, on the contrary, that it is a common thing for the wicked to prosper and the righteous to be greatly afflicted, and, they not having proved their case, he abides by his — "all things come alike to all."

Henry grants the large truth in it: temporal judgments, when they are sent abroad, fall upon good and bad alike, and the destroying angel seldom distinguishes; the sword devours Josiah as well as Ahab, and good and bad were sent together into Babylon. If the scourge slay suddenly, God is well pleased to see the same stroke that is the perdition of the wicked be the trial of the innocent, their faith found unto praise and honour and glory at 1 Peter 1:7. But Henry will not excuse the manner: there is too much passion in what Job says; when he meant that God afflicts, he ought not to have said "he destroys" the perfect and the wicked, for God does not afflict willingly; and when the spirit is heated with dispute or discontent, we have need to set a watch before the door of our lips in speaking of divine things.

The wesleyan-arminian voices confirm the observation while noting its rareness. Adam Clarke: "my own observation shows that in the course of providence the righteous and the wicked have an equal lot; when any sudden calamity comes, the innocent and the guilty fall alike," with only a few extraordinary exceptions. John Wesley marks the precise ground of the quarrel: in the other things spoken of God's greatness and justice Job does not contend with his friends, but in this one thing he must — that God sends afflictions promiscuously upon good and bad men. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line to the same sense, "there is one thing, therefore I maintain it, the innocent and the wicked he destroyeth," and read Job's swiftly passing life as itself the instance. The witnesses do not divide over the fact, only over the temper: the maxim is largely true, but Job has spoken it in the language of a man whose spirit is overheated by his grief.
23:
The thesis is pressed to its most disturbing edge, that God is unmoved by the ruin of the guiltless — "if the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent" — and here the witnesses genuinely part over the meaning of that laughter. The reformed John Gill reads the "scourge" of any sore calamity that lashes and distresses a man, God's judgments of sword, famine, pestilence, or evil beasts, coming suddenly and sweeping all before them; and he leaves the harder clause without pressing it, noting only that some restrain the slaying to the wicked and some read a gentler dealing, that the innocent are more mildly used, dispatched at once rather than left to linger. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the laughing in a wholly favourable sense: if the scourge slay suddenly and sweep down all before it, God will be well pleased to see how the same scourge which is the perdition of the wicked is the trial of the innocent and of their faith; let this reconcile God's children to their troubles, which are but trials designed for their honour and benefit, so that at destruction and famine they too may laugh, as Job had been told at Job 5:22.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same word the opposite way, as Job's dark rhetoric of a God who seems indifferent: in the case of a hidden calamity overtaking an innocent man, God will "laugh at it," take no more notice than if it furnished him with sport, so that the very fact of such calamity befalling the innocent looks, in one view, like proof of his indifference — as if he winked at what his providence could easily prevent. This, Ellicott insists, is the argument of a man who for the sake of the debate wilfully takes the pessimist view of providence, confronting friends who maintain the rigid, unfailing justice of God with the severe logic of facts they can neither contradict nor explain; and all the while, it must never be forgotten, Job holds fast his faith, so that at the last God justifies him and says his friends had not spoken of him what was right, as at Job 42:8. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley stands with the favourable reading: if some common judgment come upon a people, God will be well pleased to see the same scourge that is the perdition of the wicked prove the trial of the innocent, and of their faith, found unto praise and honour and glory. So the debate is real and unresolved: whether the God who "laughs" at the innocent's trial delights, like a refiner, in the faith that his stroke proves, or wears, in Job's overstrained speech, the face of an indifference that the sufferer flings out against the friends' too-easy justice.
24:
The complaint reaches its boldest reach in the charge that the world itself is handed over to the wrong men — "the earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covereth the faces of the judges thereof" — and the witnesses ask first who this "wicked" one is. The reformed John Gill offers a range: it may be the wicked one, Satan, the god of this world, as Jarchi and Bar Tzemach take it; or some wicked tyrant such as Nimrod, or another known to Job in his time; or wicked men in general, who for the most part have the greatest share of the earth and of power in it. And this they have of God, who disposes of the earth and its fulness as he will, so that the giving of these things is no proof of a man's goodness, nor the taking of them away any evidence of his wickedness — love and hatred are not to be known by such things. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the plain observation: is it not most evident that the worst men possess most of this world's goods, and the righteous are scarcely ever in power or affluence? So it was in Job's time, and so it is still; therefore prosperity and adversity in this life are no marks of God's approbation or disapprobation.

On the covering of the judges' faces the witnesses read a judicial blinding permitted, not wrought, by God. Clarke: God is often said in Scripture to do what he only permits to be done, so that he permits the eyes of judgment to be blinded, and hence come false decisions; and if it be not God who orders these things, who is he that does? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same reversal — as good men are frequently scourged, so the wicked are advanced; meantime God covers the faces of the wise and good, fit to be judges, and buries them alive in obscurity, perhaps suffers them to be condemned and their faces covered as criminals by those to whom the earth is given; and if it be not God who does it, where and who is he that does?

The puritan-evangelical reading holds the paradox in balance: the wicked have the earth given them, but the righteous have heaven — and which is better, heaven without earth, or earth without heaven? God in his providence advances wicked men while he covers the faces of those qualified to judge; yet, following Bishop Patrick and the Assembly's Annotations, the "wicked one" into whose hand the earth is given may be some noted tyrant then living, whose great wickedness and great prosperity were known to Job and his friends alike. The witnesses converge on the fact Job presses and divide only over the figure — Satan the god of this age, a particular tyrant, or wicked men at large — while agreeing that the disposal of the earth lies, even in this dark aspect, in the hand of him who rules in the kingdoms of men and gives them to whomsoever he will.
25:
"Now my days are swifter than a post" — the storm of argument falls away, and Job turns from God's dealings to the headlong flight of his own vanishing life. The reformed John Gill takes the "post" for a runner in a race, or one who rides post or runs on foot to carry a message, such as were Cushi and Ahimaaz, generally swift of foot or mounted on swift horses; yet Job says his days are swifter still, meaning especially, as Broughton reads it, his prosperous days, which no sooner came than they were gone. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry allows the complaint of the passing of prosperity to be proper enough: all Job's good days are gone, never to return, gone of a sudden, gone ere he was aware; never did courier with good tidings make such haste as his comforts made from him, nor does any trace of his prosperity remain, any more than of an eagle in the air or a ship in the sea, as at Proverbs 30:19. Henry draws the double lesson: how swift is the motion of time, always upon the wing, staying for no man; and how vain the enjoyments of time, of which we may be deprived while yet time continues, so that our day may be longer than the sunshine of our prosperity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the word as "a runner," the light-footed courier who carries messages from place to place, and adds the Chaldee's turn, that Job's days are swifter than the shadow of a flying bird — so swiftly do they flee that he cannot discern them, and when past they cannot be recalled; he sets beside it Virgil's line that irreparable time flies away. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the pivot of the whole passage: with "swifter than a post" Job now turns away from the contemplation of God and his dealings to that of his own misery. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "my days" as the days of his life, the "post" as one who rides upon swift horses, and "they see no good" as meaning that he enjoys no good in them, "seeing" being often put for the experiencing of good or evil.

The witnesses do not divide. They read a verse in which the sufferer, having despaired of a hearing with God, looks down at the ruin of his own span and finds it racing to its end without a backward trace — a complaint the puritan reading judges innocent enough in itself, so long as it does not pass, as it soon will, into the harder charge that God cannot be appeased; for to complain to God is allowed, but to complain of God is the language of a corruption Job will afterward be given leave to unsay.
26:
The flight of Job's days is caught in two more images, the light boat and the stooping eagle, and the witnesses linger over the puzzle of the "swift ships." The reformed John Gill takes them for vessels of the lightest build and swiftest motion; Bar Tzemach thinks of ships rowed with oars, "ships of will or desire," which may be driven at pleasure where and when a man will; others of ships so swift that they reach the haven as soon as one could wish; and Gill notes too the rendering "pirate ships," or "ships of enmity," light craft not laden with goods and therefore moving the faster. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns the phrase a mystery: what the "swift ships," or ships of Eveh, may be no one knows; the word is probably a proper name, perhaps for a particular kind of boat used on the Nile — one instance, if so, out of many of Job's acquaintance with Egypt — while the Vulgate reads "ships bearing fruit." Keil and Delitzsch render it "ships of reeds," the light papyrus skiffs that shoot down the river.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets out both the received and a variant reading. Taken as it stands, the "ships of desire" are inflated ships, their sails bellying out with a brisk fair wind, lightly freighted, and perhaps the point is not so much their swiftness as their leaving no trace or track behind them; but forty-seven of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, with the Syriac, read instead "hostile ships," the light fast vessels of pirates, so that Job's days are gone off like the corsairs' craft that, having stripped him of his property, carry all irrecoverably away under the strongest press of sail — and the next image, "as the eagle that hasteth to the prey," Clarke thinks, favours that reading, keeping the idea of robbery and spoil, of prompt attack and sudden retreat. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the eagle simply as the bird that flies most swiftly, especially in sight of its prey, and draws again the lesson of the swift motion of time and the vanity of its enjoyments.

So a real difference of reading runs beneath the verse — whether the "swift ships" are the reed-boats of the Nile, leaving no wake behind them, as Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take them, or the pirate craft that strip and flee, as Clarke's manuscripts and Gill's alternative would have it — though both amount to the one thing Job means: a life sped past beyond recall, like a boat that outruns the eye and an eagle that drops upon its quarry and is gone.
27:
Job now turns to describe his own vain effort to shake off his grief, the resolve to change his look and be cheerful that his sorrow will not let him keep. The reformed John Gill reads the first movement as Job's attempt to forget the very causes of his complaint — the loss of children, servants, substance, and health — to cease complaining, bury these things in oblivion, and change his note to another and a gladder key. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders the resolve in the same spirit: "I will forsake or forego my complaining; I will leave off my heaviness," and, with the Vulgate, "I will change my countenance," forcing himself to smile and endeavouring to assume the very appearance of comfort. It is the language of a man deliberately laying down his grief and reaching after a gladder note, resolving to bury the causes of his sorrow in oblivion and to wear again the look of one at peace.

The puritan-evangelical reading fills in the pastoral shape of the attempt. It should seem that Job did his endeavour to quiet and compose himself, as his friends advised: this was the good he would do — he would fain forget his complaints and praise God, leave off his heaviness and comfort himself, that he might be fit for converse both with God and man. It is a resolve, the puritan voice notes, easier formed than kept, for it is easier in such a case to know what we should do than to do it, and easier to preach patience to those in trouble than for them to practise it; fear and sorrow are tyrannising things, not readily brought into the subjection they ought to be kept in to religion and right reason.

The witnesses do not divide, and the little verse carries more than its length. Job is not a man indulging his misery without resistance; he sets himself deliberately to lay down his complaint, to smooth his brow, to speak and look as one comforted — which is precisely the counsel his friends have been urging, and which he honestly tries. That the attempt collapses, as the next verse will tell, is no proof that he did not make it; rather it measures the depth of a trouble that overpowers even the will to be free of it, so that the resolution to forget his complaint is itself swallowed up by the return of the very sorrows he had resolved to forget.
28:
The resolve of the moment before breaks at once upon the fear that his sufferings will not release him — "I am afraid of all my sorrows; I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent." The reformed John Gill reads the dread of their return and continuance: Job feared that all his sorrows would come back upon him, surround and overwhelm him, so that he should not be able to stand up under them, but that they would increase and abide, and he should never be released. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears a further and finer fear in the words, following the older versions: "even were I to cease from complaining, I am afraid of all my works," lest not one of them, however well intentioned, should stand God's scrutiny or meet his approbation; and the closing clause he takes to mean not that God favours no evil-doer, but that God "will not acquit me so as to take away my afflictions from me."

The puritan-evangelical reading joins the two halves of the verse into the honest confession of a man who cannot do what he had just resolved. Job would fain have forgotten his complaint and comforted himself, but he found he could not: "I am afraid of all my sorrows; when I strive most against my trouble, it prevails most over me and proves too hard for me." The endeavour to be cheerful is defeated by the sheer weight of the grief, so that the fear he had meant to master rises up and masters him.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the ground of the second clause, where Job makes a sudden address to God: all such endeavours to compose himself are vain, for though his griefs be suspended a while, his fears continue; and he plainly perceives that God will not clear his innocency by removing the afflictions that make his friends judge him guilty of some great crime — "words," Wesley adds, "proceeding from despair and impatience." The witnesses do not divide. They read a verse in which Job's brave resolve to forget his sorrow is broken by two fears at once — that the sorrow will never end, and that God will never publicly acquit him — and they mark, without excusing it, the impatience that has begun to color his thoughts of God, even as they own the reality of the anguish that has bred it.
29:
Job draws the bitter conclusion that, since he is to be treated as guilty whatever he does, his striving to clear himself is labour thrown away — "if I be wicked, why then labour I in vain?" The reformed John Gill offers two readings of the line. It may mean that if Job be the wicked hypocrite his friends took him for, it is vain to make supplication to God, as they advised, for God hears not sinners who regard iniquity in their hearts; prayer, which is a striving and wrestling with God, would then be lost labour. But rather, Gill judges, the sense is that if Job is accounted wicked in God's dealing with him — if God will not hold him innocent, as the last verse said — then it is in vain for him to labour to prove his integrity, since the verdict is already fixed against him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of the vanity of feigning cheerfulness: "if I am the sinner you suppose me to be, in vain should I labour to counterfeit joy and cease to complain of my sufferings" — the effort of the two preceding verses would be idle, for the misery would remain. The puritan-evangelical reading presses the "why then do I labour in vain?" as the cry of a man who despairs of redress: it is to no purpose to speak in a cause already prejudged, and with men it is often labour lost for the most innocent to go about to clear themselves, since they must be adjudged guilty though the evidence be ever so plain for them.

Yet the same puritan voice sets against Job's despair the truth he has for the moment forgotten: it is not so in our dealings with God, who is the patron of oppressed innocency, and to whom it was never in vain to commit a righteous cause. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the whole in that key of hopelessness — "I shall be used like a wicked man still; why then should I comfort myself with vain hopes of deliverance, as thou advisest me?" The witnesses do not divide over the sense: whether the labour be prayer, or the counterfeiting of joy, or the pleading of his own case, Job reckons it all wasted so long as God will not openly declare him innocent — a conclusion the sources let stand as the real language of his grief, while quietly reminding the reader that the righteous cause committed to God is never, in the end, committed in vain.
30:
The despair of clearing himself takes a vivid figure from the washing that cannot make him clean — "if I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean, yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch." The reformed John Gill reads it of the utter insufficiency of any self-cleansing: let Job take what methods he will to purge himself, they are all in vain, his iniquity will still be marked before God. Snow water was reckoned the best for whitening the skin and contracting the pores; but there is nothing a man can do — no ceremonial ablution, such as may have been used before the law of Moses, nor moral duty, nor even repentance — that can make him pure in the sight of a holy God, for these can sanctify but the flesh, and cannot purify the heart so as to leave no more conscience of sin. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes that snow water was thought to have a more detergent quality and was preferred to common water by the ancients, and finds here, with Mr. Good, an allusion to the ancient rite of washing the hands in token of innocence, as in Psalm 26:6, "I will wash my hands in innocency," and as Pilate declared himself guiltless of the blood of Christ at Matthew 27:24.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence into the strophe it opens: though Job wash with snow water and cleanse his hands with lye, yet God would plunge him into the pit, and his own clothes would abhor him; for God is not a man, as he is, that he should answer him, nor is there an arbitrator between them who might lay his hand upon them both. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the washing plainly of Job's clearing himself of all imputations and fully proving his innocency before men — which, the verse goes on to say, would still avail nothing before God.

The puritan-evangelical reading turns the figure to its searching use. If we be ever so industrious to justify ourselves before men, and keep our hands ever so clean from the gross sins that fall under the world's eye, yet God, who knows our hearts, can charge us with so much secret sin as will for ever take off all our pretensions to purity, and make us see ourselves odious in the sight of the holy God — as Paul, while a Pharisee, made his hands very clean, but when the commandment came and discovered his heart-sins, was plunged in the ditch. The witnesses do not divide; they read a man who feels that no cleansing of his own can answer the purity of God, and who therefore despairs — half in truth, half in the passion of his grief — of ever appearing clean before his Judge.
31:
The washing figure completes itself in a picture of loathsome defilement, God plunging the cleansed man into the pit till his own garments shrink from him. The reformed John Gill reads the "ditch" first in a spiritual sense, the filthy pit of sin in which the unregenerate lie and to which the hypocrite returns; yet Job was neither unregenerate nor hypocrite nor self-righteous, and the meaning is that, set against the perfect purity and holiness of God, he should appear exceedingly impure, and God would treat him so, holding him out to the view of others as the filth of the world by continuing his afflictions. Or, Gill adds, by the "ditch" may be meant the ditch of affliction itself — his present filthy ulcers and scabs, or new and deeper troubles into which God would bring him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole of God's infinite purity set over against man's: searched and tried by the eye of God, Job would be found as a leper, so that his own clothes would dread to touch him for fear of infection — a strong and bold figure drawn, Clarke thinks, from the corrupt state of Job's body, which his very clothes shrank from because of the contagion of his disease.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it to the same effect: God would prove Job a most guilty creature, notwithstanding all his purity before men, so filthy that his own clothes, if they had any sense in them, would abhor to touch him. The puritan-evangelical reading takes the plunging into the ditch as Job's own bitter reading of his afflictions, the very things that blackened him in the eyes of his friends: he saw them coming from God, and complained of their continuance as the ruin not only of his comfort but of his reputation, so that though he washed himself ever so clean, judgment must still go against him, and he would be made so offensive that his own clothes should abhor him.

Yet the same reading rescues a good sense from the hard words. If we be ever so careful to justify ourselves before men and to keep our hands from open sin, God, who knows the heart, can charge us with secret sin enough to plunge us in the ditch — as the commandment did to Paul the Pharisee when it discovered lust in him. The witnesses do not divide over the figure of a defilement no washing can prevent; they only weigh how much of it is the sober truth that no flesh is clean before God, and how much the exaggeration of a sufferer who feels God's hand set, past all appeasing, against him.
32:
"For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him" — Job names at last the root of his whole helplessness, the infinite distance between the creature and his Maker that makes a fair trial impossible. The reformed John Gill unfolds the disparity: though the parts of a human body are sometimes ascribed to God, these are spoken after the manner of men, for he is a Spirit, infinite, immortal, invisible, pure and holy, just and true and without iniquity; whereas Job is but a man, a finite, feeble, mortal, and sinful creature. The potsherds may strive and contend with the potsherds of the earth, their equals, but not with God their Creator, who is more than a match for them, sees impurity where man sees none, and can bring a charge and support it where the creature thought there was nothing to answer; and therefore it is a vain thing to litigate a point with him or attempt to vindicate one's innocence before him.

The puritan-evangelical reading grounds the same complaint in a settled truth and turns it to humility. Job could venture to dispute with a man like himself — the potsherds may strive with the potsherds of the earth — but God is infinitely above him, and he dare not enter the lists. Of the greatest princes we may say, "they are men as we are," but not of the great God, whose thoughts and ways are infinitely above ours, and whom we must not measure by ourselves; man is foolish and weak, frail and fickle, but God is not, for we are dying creatures and he the immortal Creator. And the consideration of this, the puritan voice adds, should keep us very humble and very silent before God: let us not make ourselves equal with him, but always eye him as infinitely above us.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the verse the same way, that God is not a man but one infinitely superior in majesty, power, wisdom, and justice, so that Job should not presume to debate his cause with him, nor come, as it were, face to face to plead upon equal terms. The witnesses do not divide. They read the plainest statement of the chapter's whole difficulty: the reason Job cannot answer, cannot be justified in argument, cannot obtain a hearing, is not that God is unjust, but that God is God and Job is dust — a disparity so vast that it turns the very thought of a lawsuit between them into presumption, and leaves the creature no posture but silence, or supplication, before a Judge who is not a man as he is.
33:
"Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both" — from the disparity Job passes to the lack that most galls him, that between so great a God and so mean a man there stands no umpire to hold the scales. The reformed John Gill explains the office wished for: a "daysman" is one who, hearing a cause, reproves him that is found in the wrong, or an arbitrator to whom the case may be referred; but such a one must be both wiser and mightier than the two he judges between, and there is none among angels or men wiser and mightier than God, so that no umpire can be found capable of standing between Job and his Maker.
