The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the legal term — a "daysman" is, in the old law, an arbitrator or umpire appointed by consent of both parties to judge between them and settle their differences — and then marks a striking variant: for the received "there is not," fifteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic, read "O that there were!" so that the line becomes a wish, "O that we had a mediator, an advocate and judge between us both!" Poor Job, Clarke adds, did not yet know the Mediator between God and man; had he this in view, one thinks of Paul's word at 1 Timothy 2:5, that there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the "daysman" as an umpire whose part is to lay his hand upon both, to order and govern them in the pleading and oblige them to stand to his decision; and he too lifts the eye to the answer the Gospel gives — that the Lord Jesus is now the blessed daysman who has mediated between heaven and earth and laid his hand upon us both, though this was not made so clear then as it is now, which leaves no room for such a complaint as Job's.

The puritan-evangelical reading hears in the complaint that there is none a wish that there were, and takes the Septuagint's reading — "O that there were a mediator between us!" — to the same conclusion: Job would gladly refer the matter, but no creature was capable of being the referee, and so he must refer it still to God himself and acquiesce in his judgment. Our Lord Jesus, the puritan voice affirms, is that blessed daysman, who has laid his hand upon both, to whom the Father has committed all judgment; but the matter was not then brought to the light the Gospel now gives. The witnesses do not divide; they read a real cry for an arbiter, and turn its very absence in Job's day into a pointer toward the Mediator whom the Gospel would reveal.
34:
Job frames the one condition on which he could bear to plead — that God would first lift the crushing rod and lay aside the terror of his majesty. The reformed John Gill is careful to say what rod Job means: not the government of God, of which the rod or sceptre is the ensign, for Job did not wish to be freed from that, but the rod of affliction, the stroke of his hand, which lay so heavy upon him and so depressed his spirit that he could not, while it remained, reason freely about his case, and for the removing of which he here prays. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes the Masoretic curiosity that the word for "his rod" is written with a large letter, which the Masora explains as marking the nine calamities under which Job had suffered and wished removed; and since the same word signifies a sceptre, the ensign of royalty, Clarke thinks Job may refer to God sitting in his majesty upon the judgment-seat, a sight so appalling that, filled with terror, he is unable to speak — as Isaiah, seeing the Lord high and lifted up, cried, "Woe is me, for I am undone," at Isaiah 6.

The puritan-evangelical reading takes the "rod" less of Job's outward affliction than of the load upon his spirit from the apprehension of God's wrath: that was the fear which terrified him, and he asks that it be removed — "let me recover the sight of his mercy, and not be amazed with nothing but his terrors, and then I would speak and order my cause before him." The trouble is that it is not so with him; the cloud is not dissipated, the sense of God's displeasure still preys upon his spirits, and what to do he knows not.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the "fear" as the dread of God's majesty and justice, and the prayer as a plea for grace over strict justice: "let him not deal with me according to his perfect justice, but according to his grace and clemency." The witnesses do not divide. They read a sufferer who does not ask to escape God's rule but only for a space of relief from the weight of his hand and the terror of his greatness, that he might gather himself to speak; and beneath the request they hear the true source of his distress — not the boils and losses only, but the apprehension of an angry God, which the sight of mercy alone could lift.
35:
The chapter ends on the condition unfulfilled, the speech Job could make if only the terror were gone, and the plain confession that it is not — "then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me." The reformed John Gill reads the freedom Job longs for as the boldness of a man before whom the rod and the dread of majesty have been removed: were that terror lifted, he could speak without a servile fear, though still with reverence, so as to defend himself and make his cause appear just. He hears too a deeper note, of the liberty a believer has at the throne of grace through the Mediator, when the terror of justice is taken away and the favour of God shown; but Job's own sense is chiefly that, so long as the dread lay on him, he could not tell his case as it was or use his arguments to advantage. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the close simply, "then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me" — the two conditions of the verse before, that God take away his rod and let not his terror stupefy him, being followed by the resolve to speak, which the last clause at once withdraws.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the final words as the surrender of a man not in a case to plead: "I am not in such circumstances as to plead with my Judge," and he prizes Coverdale's turn, "for as long as I am in such fearfulness, I can make no answer" — a natural picture, he says, of a penitent soul, which needs no additional colouring, since when a sinful soul sees God in his majesty, terror seizes it and prayer becomes impossible. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns the closing phrase variously understood: literally "I am not so with me," it may mean "I am not thus without fear," as the first half of the verse supposes; or "I am not so as ye suppose," that is, not guilty, but innocent; or "am I not right with myself?" — inwardly conscious of an integrity he cannot make good before God, the very self-consciousness he will voice again at Job 10:1.

The witnesses do not finally divide; they read a chapter that ends where it must, on a note of unresolved longing. Job knows what he would say if he could stand before God unafraid, and knows that he cannot so stand; the rod is not lifted, the terror not withdrawn, and so the speech he could make dies on his lips. Whether the last words confess a fear he cannot shake, or quietly maintain the innocence his friends deny, or reach after a self that has become a riddle to him, they leave the sufferer suspended between a plea he cannot bring and a Judge he cannot approach — the very impasse from which, in the chapters to follow, the cry for a daysman will keep breaking out.
